bargaining_script: ಇದು ಎಷ್ಟು? (how much?) → ತುಂಬಾ ದುಬಾರಿ! (too pricey!) → ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ ಕಡಿಮೆ ಮಾಡಿ (reduce a little) → ರಿಯಾಯಿತಿ ಕೊಡಿ (give a discount) → ಸರಿ, ಪ್ಯಾಕ್ ಮಾಡಿ! (done, pack it!)

counting_note: Kannada has no classifiers — put the number straight before the noun. But the noun itself goes plural with -ಗಳು: ಒಂದು ಪುಸ್ತಕ (one book), ಎರಡು ಪುಸ್ತಕಗಳು (two books), ಮೂರು ರೂಪಾಯಿ (three rupees).

culture.en: The maharaja's palace in Mysuru — lit with a lakh of bulbs on Sundays and through Dasara.
Karnataka's royal festival (Sep–Oct) — the Mysuru procession with caparisoned elephants.

gender_note: Kannada has three genders: masculine (ಅವನು, he), feminine (ಅವಳು, she) and neuter (ಅದು — animals, things, babies). Only third-person verbs show gender: ತಿನ್ನುತ್ತಾನೆ/ತಿನ್ನುತ್ತಾಳೆ/ತಿನ್ನುತ್ತದೆ (he/she/it eats). 'I' and 'you' never change: ನಾನು ತಿನ್ನುತ್ತೇನೆ suits every speaker.

greetings.note: works any time of day, for everyone

name: Kannada
negation_note: ಇಲ್ಲ (illa) melts into the verb: ಬರುವುದಿಲ್ಲ (won't come / doesn't come), ಗೊತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ (don't know), ಮಾಡುವುದಿಲ್ಲ (won't do). Alone, ಇಲ್ಲ just means 'no'. To refuse an offer, ಬೇಡ (bēḍa — 'don't want') is warmer: ಕಾಫಿ ಬೇಡ (no coffee for me, thanks).

postpositions.ex_en: The book is on the table.

present_note: The present is stem + -ಉತ್ತ- + ending: -ಏನೆ (I), -ಈಯೆ (ನೀನು), -ಈರಿ (ನೀವು), -ಆನೆ/-ಆಳೆ/-ಅದೆ (he/she/it), -ಏವೆ (we), -ಆರೆ (they). So ನಾನು ತಿನ್ನುತ್ತೇನೆ (I eat), ನೀವು ತಿನ್ನುತ್ತೀರಿ (you eat, respectful), ಅವರು ತಿನ್ನುತ್ತಾರೆ (they eat). In quick speech the endings blur — listen for the -ಉತ್ತ- core.

ನೀವು ಊಟ ಮಾಡಿದಿರಾ? — 'have you eaten?' — is asked like 'how are you', with real warmth.
ಮತ್ತೆ ಸಿಗೋಣ (matte sigōṇa) — literally 'we'll meet again' — the warm goodbye.
ಪುಸ್ತಕ (pustaka) = book — ಲೇಖನಿ is the old word for pen.
ಸ್ನೇಹಿತ (snēhita) = friend — ಗೆಳೆಯ is the casual 'buddy'.
ಇದು ಎಷ್ಟು? = how much is this — then counter with ಸ್ವಲ್ಪ ಕಡಿಮೆ ಮಾಡಿ!
ನಾಳೆ (nāḷe) = tomorrow; ನಿನ್ನೆ (ninne) = yesterday. Don't mix them at the station!

script_note: Kannada's letters are famously round — the script was written with a stylus on palm leaves, and straight lines would have torn the leaf. It runs left to right with no headline bar, and it is beautifully phonetic: each letter is one sound, always. There are 13 vowels (ಅ ಆ ಇ ಈ ಉ ಊ ಋ ಎ ಏ ಐ ಒ ಓ ಔ, plus ಅಂ/ಅಃ for nasalization) and 34 consonants. Letters join into conjuncts (ಒತ್ತಕ್ಷರ): ಕ + ್ + ಣ = ಕ್ಷಣ (kshaṇa, moment). Close cousin of the Telugu script — learn one and the other looks familiar.
